articles.title: It Isn't Just the Calories: Ultra-Processed Diets Are Now Linked to Falling Male Fertility
articles.excerpt: A tightly controlled feeding study found that just three weeks on an ultra-processed diet worsened body fat, blood lipids and hormones tied to sperm production — even when calories and nutrients were matched — pointing the finger at industrial processing itself.
articles.image_caption: A controlled study links ultra-processed diets to hormonal changes affecting sperm production in young men
articles.nri_angle: Falling fertility and rising reliance on packaged convenience food are both acute in diaspora life — long work hours, ready meals and Western supermarket aisles displacing home-cooked dals and vegetables — making this a quietly personal warning for younger NRI couples already navigating the cost and stress of fertility treatment abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A High-Dose Omega-3 Pill Reached the Brain but Did Nothing for Memory, a Gold-Standard Trial Finds
articles.excerpt: In a two-year randomized trial of older adults at risk of dementia, daily fish-oil-style DHA more than doubled omega-3 levels in the blood and reached the brain — yet it failed to improve memory, thinking or the size of the brain’s memory centre any more than a placebo.
articles.image_caption: Omega-3 fish-oil capsules; a two-year randomized trial found high-dose DHA reached the brain but did not improve memory
articles.nri_angle: Fish-oil and omega-3 capsules are among the most popular over-the-counter supplements in Indian-origin households, often bought in bulk and taken for years in the belief they protect the aging brain; this rigorous trial is a reminder that for most people the money may be better spent on diet and exercise than on a daily pill.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It May Not Be How Much Protein You Eat, but Which Building Blocks — a New Longevity-Diet Study Suggests
articles.excerpt: Scientists at USC report that fine-tuning a single amino acid, methionine, let mice eat more food yet lose fat without losing muscle — and that people eating the most animal protein had twice the rate of diabetes, hinting the kind of protein may matter more than the amount.
articles.image_caption: Lentils and legumes; new research suggests the type of protein, not just the amount, may shape metabolic health
articles.nri_angle: The protein debate cuts to the heart of diaspora eating habits — from the dal-and-rice plant-based traditions of many Indian households to the high-protein, meat-heavy regimes popular in Western fitness culture — and this research suggests the traditional emphasis on plant proteins may carry an underappreciated metabolic advantage.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Joint-Pain Supplement Millions Take May Quietly Speed Up Alzheimer’s, a New Study Warns
articles.excerpt: A study in Nature Metabolism finds that glucosamine — one of the world’s most popular supplements for aching knees — fuels a sugar build-up in the brain that worsened memory in mice and was tied to faster decline and higher death rates in people with dementia.
articles.image_caption: Dietary supplement capsules; a new study links glucosamine to a sugar build-up that worsened Alzheimer’s in mice and people
articles.nri_angle: Glucosamine is a staple in the supplement cabinets of older Indian-origin adults managing arthritis and knee pain, often taken for years without a doctor’s oversight; this study is an early but sobering signal that anyone in a diaspora family already living with memory loss should review the habit with a physician rather than assume a 'natural' joint pill is harmless.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Four Minutes a Day Was Enough to Make Frail Older Adults Steadier on Their Feet, a Trial Finds
articles.excerpt: A home-based program of just four simple exercises — done daily for half a minute each — measurably improved leg strength, balance and the ability to rise from a chair in inactive adults over 65, with most participants sticking to it 81 percent of the time.
articles.image_caption: An older adult exercising at home; a four-minute daily routine improved balance and leg strength in adults over 65
articles.nri_angle: Aging Indian-origin parents — many living with their children abroad, often sedentary through long winters and culturally hesitant about gyms — are precisely the group this study targets: a four-minute, no-equipment-heavy routine doable in a living room is a realistic way for diaspora families to help elders stay independent and avoid the falls that so often trigger a cascade of decline.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Why Poor Sleep Harms Some Brains More Than Others May Come Down to a Single Gene
articles.excerpt: A new study of a brain-cleaning gene called AQP4 found that the same sleep habits can speed or slow early Alzheimer's-type changes depending on which version of the gene a person carries — a clue to why two people who sleep alike can age so differently.
articles.image_caption: A normal brain compared with an Alzheimer's-affected brain; a gene called AQP4 may shape how sleep affects early decline (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Sleep is one of the few dementia risk factors anyone can actually change, and for a diaspora that often runs on jet lag, late shifts and a strong family history of dementia, the finding that a person's genes decide how much their sleep matters is a practical nudge to treat rest as preventive medicine, not a luxury.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Dangerous Heat Now Reaches More of the World — and the Nights Are No Longer a Refuge
articles.excerpt: A new analysis finds the share of the planet exposed to severe heat stress climbed from 16% to 22% over fifty years, with brutal heat spreading into regions that never knew it and ‘tropical nights’ stripping away the body's chance to cool down and recover.
articles.image_caption: A new study finds severe heat stress now reaches 22% of the world's population, up from 16% five decades ago
articles.nri_angle: Heat is a health story that bridges the diaspora's two worlds at once — family in Indian cities enduring some of the planet's most punishing summers, and relatives in the UK, North America and Scandinavia now facing heat their homes were never built for, making this a rare risk that touches both ends of the migration journey.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Weight-Loss Drug That Was Feared to Weaken Bones May Actually Help Protect Them
articles.excerpt: In a study of nearly 60,000 adults with type 2 diabetes, those on semaglutide — the drug behind Ozempic and Wegovy — broke fewer bones than people on rival weight-loss treatments, easing a long-standing worry that rapid weight loss leaves the skeleton fragile.
articles.image_caption: A study of nearly 60,000 diabetes patients found semaglutide users had a lower fracture rate than those on rival weight-loss drugs
articles.nri_angle: Indians carry one of the world's heaviest burdens of type 2 diabetes and are increasingly being prescribed GLP-1 drugs in India and abroad — so reassurance that semaglutide does not appear to crumble the bones of diabetic patients, and may even guard them, speaks directly to millions of NRI families weighing whether a parent or partner should start one of these medicines.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Common Vitamin in Citrus and Greens Is Linked to a Better-Preserved Brain in Older Age
articles.excerpt: In more than 2,000 older adults, those with higher blood levels of vitamin C had more grey matter and stronger memory-network connections on brain scans — the first study to tie measured vitamin C, not just diet surveys, to the brain's structure.
articles.image_caption: Citrus, amla, tomatoes and leafy greens are among the richest dietary sources of vitamin C, linked to better-preserved brain structure
articles.nri_angle: Indian cuisine is rich in the very foods that deliver vitamin C — amla, citrus, guava, tomatoes, green chillies and leafy saag — yet long cooking and changing diets can strip it away, making this a timely, low-cost reminder for diaspora families that protecting an ageing parent's mind may start with what is on the plate.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: One of the Biggest Risks for Dementia Is Also One of the Easiest to Treat — and It Sits in the Ears
articles.excerpt: A new analysis of more than 16,000 American adults found severe hearing loss was associated with a sharply higher risk of dementia, while a major randomized trial showed that simply fitting at-risk elders with hearing aids slowed their cognitive decline by nearly half.
articles.image_caption: Researchers found fitting at-risk older adults with hearing aids cut their rate of cognitive decline by nearly half
articles.nri_angle: In many Indian families, an elder's fading hearing is quietly accepted as a normal part of getting old and rarely treated — yet this research reframes an untreated hearing problem as a serious, fixable threat to the mind, making a hearing test and a pair of hearing aids one of the most worthwhile gifts an NRI child can arrange for a parent ageing in India or abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Scientists Have Found Microplastics Inside the Human Eye — and the More There Were, the Higher the Pressure
articles.excerpt: In the first study to look, researchers detected microplastic particles in every sample of a delicate drainage tissue taken from glaucoma patients, and the plastic burden tracked closely with the dangerously high eye pressure that drives the disease.
articles.image_caption: Scientists detected microplastic particles in the eye's fluid-draining tissue, linked to higher intraocular pressure in glaucoma patients
articles.nri_angle: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness in India, and the diaspora hails from some of the most plastic-saturated, air-polluted cities on earth — so early evidence that plastic particles may lodge in the eye and push up the pressure that steals sight is a story that lands close to home for millions of NRI families.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Weakness That Comes With Age May Live as Much in the Brain as in the Muscle, a New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: When researchers gave older adults a jolt of electrical stimulation at the moment they thought they were pushing as hard as they could, the weakest among them produced far more force — a sign that ageing nerves, not just shrinking muscle, may be holding strength back.
articles.image_caption: A study of 66 older adults found weaker participants had untapped muscle strength their nervous systems were not fully activating
articles.nri_angle: For NRI families caring for ageing parents across continents — often advising on health by video call — the finding reframes the goal from simply lifting weights to keeping the brain-to-muscle connection sharp, suggesting that balance work, coordination and learning new movements deserve a place alongside resistance training in the routines that keep elders independent.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: People on Ozempic-Style Drugs Are Moving Less, Not More — and Doctors Say That Undercuts the Benefit
articles.excerpt: A study of 753 adults using fitness-tracker data found that daily steps and exercise actually fell after people started GLP-1 weight-loss medications, raising the risk that muscle is lost along with fat unless physical activity is built in deliberately.
articles.image_caption: A study of 753 adults found daily steps and exercise fell after people began GLP-1 weight-loss medications
articles.nri_angle: GLP-1 drugs have spread fast among diaspora Indians battling the high rates of diabetes and obesity that run in South Asian families, and this finding is a pointed warning — for a group already prone to losing muscle and storing dangerous fat, taking the medication without keeping up movement risks trading one health problem for another.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: How Fit You Are in Midlife May Forecast How Long — and How Well — You Live, a 24,000-Person Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Adults with higher cardiorespiratory fitness measured on a treadmill in midlife went on to live longer, fall ill less often and stretch out their healthy years, according to a large analysis published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology.
articles.image_caption: A 24,576-adult study found that higher cardiorespiratory fitness in midlife was linked to a longer life span and fewer diseases
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry an outsized burden of heart disease and diabetes, often at lower body weights than other groups, and aerobic fitness is one of the few levers that pushes back on both — making this evidence that a midlife habit of brisk movement can buy healthy years especially relevant to NRI families.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Body's ‘Biological Age’ May Start Falling in Just Four Weeks on a Plant-Forward Diet, a New Trial Suggests
articles.excerpt: Older adults who shifted toward complex carbohydrates and more plant-based foods narrowed the gap between their biological and chronological age within a month — a sign that the body's ageing markers can move surprisingly fast.
articles.image_caption: A four-week trial found that shifting toward plant-forward, complex-carbohydrate diets narrowed the gap between biological and chronological age
articles.nri_angle: Traditional Indian cooking is already built around the plant-forward, complex-carbohydrate foods this trial favoured — lentils, vegetables, whole grains and legumes — meaning many diaspora families are a few deliberate swaps, not a wholesale overhaul, away from a diet linked to younger biological ageing.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Health Benefits of Coffee May Hinge on the Clock: Morning Drinkers Lived Longer in a 40,000-Person Study
articles.excerpt: People who confined their coffee to the hours before noon had the sharpest reductions in death from any cause — and from heart disease — while all-day sippers saw no such benefit, a large U.S. analysis published in the European Heart Journal found.
articles.image_caption: A large U.S. study found that adults who drank coffee only in the morning had lower rates of death than all-day drinkers
articles.nri_angle: Coffee and chai are woven into the rhythm of Indian and diaspora households — the morning cup, the evening catch-up, the late-night work fuel — and this research suggests that simply pulling caffeine earlier in the day, rather than giving it up, may be the cheapest longevity tweak an NRI can make.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: More Than 1 in 3 Older Adults Fall Short on Protein — and Vegetarians and Meal-Skippers Are Most at Risk
articles.excerpt: Despite a cultural obsession with high-protein everything, large dietary surveys keep finding that a third or more of adults over 50 miss the mark — a shortfall tied to weaker muscles, more frailty and poorer diets overall, and one that hits plant-forward eaters hardest.
articles.image_caption: Lentils, beans and other legumes are dense, affordable protein sources, key for older adults and vegetarians at risk of falling short
articles.nri_angle: A large share of the Indian diaspora eats vegetarian or near-vegetarian, leans on carbohydrate-heavy staples like rice and roti, and skips or front-loads meals around busy work and fasting schedules — exactly the pattern that leaves older adults short on protein and vulnerable to muscle loss, making this a quietly urgent issue in NRI homes.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Bacteria in Your Mouth Help Beetroot Lower Blood Pressure — and It Works Best as You Age
articles.excerpt: Two new studies show that nitrate-rich vegetables like beetroot reshape the oral microbiome to ease blood pressure in older adults, and that a surprising trick — chewing ordinary sugary gum — can amplify the effect.
articles.image_caption: Nitrate-rich beetroot lowers blood pressure with the help of bacteria in the mouth, and the effect is strongest in older adults (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: High blood pressure is one of the most common and dangerous chronic conditions in the Indian diaspora, and the foods at the heart of this research — beetroot, leafy greens and other nitrate-rich vegetables — are already fixtures of the South Asian kitchen, offering NRI families a low-cost, drug-free lever that grows more effective with age.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Lesser-Known Estrogen Made in Body Fat May Explain Why Obesity Drives Breast Cancer After Menopause
articles.excerpt: Scientists are zeroing in on estrone, a hormone churned out by fat tissue, as a hidden engine of postmenopausal breast cancer — and the finding helps explain why weight, and the new generation of weight-loss drugs, may matter more for risk than once thought.
articles.image_caption: Researchers are focusing on estrone, an estrogen produced by body fat, to explain why obesity raises postmenopausal breast cancer risk
articles.nri_angle: South Asian women carry a rising burden of both central obesity and breast cancer that often strikes earlier than in Western populations, yet awareness of the link between body fat and hormone-driven tumors remains low in many diaspora households — making the science of estrone a timely, actionable nudge toward waistline and metabolic health, not just mammograms.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Diet Built to Lower Blood Pressure Just Beat Five Rivals at Protecting the Aging Brain
articles.excerpt: In a Harvard-led comparison of nearly 160,000 people, the DASH eating pattern outperformed the Mediterranean diet and four others, with the most faithful followers showing a 41 percent lower risk of cognitive decline decades later.
articles.image_caption: A Harvard-led study found the DASH eating pattern was the strongest dietary predictor of late-life cognitive health
articles.nri_angle: South Asians face an unusually high burden of both hypertension and dementia, yet the brain-protective DASH pattern — heavy on vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and low-fat dairy, light on salt and sweets — maps neatly onto a thoughtfully built Indian thali, giving NRI families a culturally familiar template that may guard the heart and the mind at once.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: People Born With Naturally Lower Cholesterol Are Far Less Likely to Develop Dementia, a Million-Person Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Using genetics to sidestep the bias of ordinary diet studies, researchers found that a modest lifelong reduction in cholesterol — the same effect statins aim for — was linked to a sharply lower risk of dementia, hinting that protecting the heart may also protect the mind.
articles.image_caption: A study of more than a million people linked genetically lower cholesterol to a sharply reduced risk of dementia
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry both elevated heart-disease risk and a high genetic predisposition to unhealthy cholesterol, and statins are already among the most prescribed drugs in Indian households — so evidence that lifelong lower cholesterol may also guard against dementia gives the diaspora one more reason to take a number they were already told to watch seriously.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Diet and Exercise Beat a Popular Diabetes Pill at Holding Off Multiple Diseases, a 21-Year Trial Finds
articles.excerpt: Following adults with prediabetes for more than two decades, researchers found that an intensive diet-and-exercise program — not the widely prescribed drug metformin — was tied to a meaningfully lower risk of piling up multiple chronic illnesses, with the sharpest protection against the costliest disease combinations.
articles.image_caption: A 21-year trial found an intensive diet-and-exercise program lowered the long-term risk of multiple chronic diseases (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Metformin is one of the most commonly prescribed drugs across Indian households at home and abroad, and many NRIs reach for the pill while treating diet and exercise as optional — so a 21-year trial showing that the lifestyle program, not the drug, blunted the long-term accumulation of chronic disease reframes what genuine prevention looks like for a diaspora at high metabolic risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Cutting Out Sugar Entirely May Backfire on the Gut, a New Study Suggests — the Lesson Is Moderation, Not Zero
articles.excerpt: Mice fed a low-fat diet with no sugar at all developed a disrupted gut microbiome, worse blood-sugar control and signs of fatty liver — even though they did not gain weight — hinting that total elimination, rather than simply trimming excess, can undo the very benefits people are chasing.
articles.image_caption: A new study suggests removing sugar entirely from a low-fat diet may disrupt the gut microbiome (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: "Sugar-free" and "no sugar" have become aspirational badges in diaspora kitchens and on diabetes-conscious Indian menus, where cutting out mithai and refined carbs is treated as an unalloyed good — so a study warning that total elimination may disrupt gut and metabolic health adds a needed note of nuance for a community both highly sugar-aware and highly diabetes-prone.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Hours of Lifting a Week May Be a Sweet Spot for Living Longer, a 147,000-Person Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Tracking more than 147,000 American adults for up to three decades, researchers found that 90 to 120 minutes of strength training each week was tied to a 13 percent lower risk of dying from any cause — with sharper drops for heart and neurological disease, and, tellingly, no extra payoff for grinding out more than two hours.
articles.image_caption: A new study links 90 to 120 minutes of weekly strength training to a lower risk of death from all causes
articles.nri_angle: Indians abroad carry an outsized burden of diabetes and heart disease, and the gyms many already pay for go underused — so a study pinpointing two hours of weekly lifting as a longevity sweet spot offers the diaspora a concrete, time-boxed target rather than a vague call to 'exercise more.'
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: How Old Do You Feel? Your Answer May Reveal How Well You're Sleeping, a New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: In more than 3,100 adults, those who felt older than their actual age reported markedly worse sleep — more insomnia, less regular sleep and greater daytime fatigue — and, through that poor sleep, worse physical health, suggesting a single honest question can flag a problem long before a clinic visit does.
articles.image_caption: Adults who felt older than their actual age reported more insomnia and poorer sleep, a new study found
articles.nri_angle: Chronically short, late and irregular nights are almost a way of life in the diaspora — split between work hours here and family calls to India — so a study showing that simply feeling older than your years is an early warning sign of poor sleep gives NRIs a quick, free self-check before fatigue hardens into ill health.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Fish-Oil Pills Did Reach the Brain — but Did Nothing for Memory, a Two-Year Trial of At-Risk Adults Finds
articles.excerpt: In a rigorous double-blind study, high doses of the omega-3 DHA clearly raised omega-3 levels in the brains of older adults at risk for Alzheimer's, yet brought no improvement in memory, thinking or the shrinkage of the brain's memory centre — a sobering result for a supplement Americans spend over a billion dollars a year on.
articles.image_caption: A two-year trial found high-dose omega-3 DHA reached the brain but did not improve memory in adults at risk for Alzheimer's
articles.nri_angle: Fish-oil capsules are a fixture of the diaspora medicine cabinet — reached for as cheap insurance for the brain, especially in largely vegetarian Indian households that eat little oily fish — so a gold-standard trial showing the pills do not protect memory is a pointed reminder for NRI families to spend on the lifestyle basics that do, rather than on a supplement that does not.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Daily Multivitamin Modestly Slowed the Body's Biological Clock in a Two-Year Trial — but the Effect Was Small
articles.excerpt: Using 'epigenetic clocks' that read the chemical wear on DNA, researchers found older adults who took a daily multivitamin with cocoa flavanols for two years aged slightly more slowly at the cellular level than those on a placebo — a tantalising but modest result that sits alongside stronger evidence for diet and fitness.
articles.image_caption: A two-year trial linked a daily multivitamin with cocoa flavanols to a modest slowing of biological ageing on epigenetic clocks
articles.nri_angle: Multivitamins are a staple of NRI households — mailed to students abroad and pressed on ageing parents — so evidence that the pills nudge biological ageing only modestly, while diet and fitness move it far more, helps the diaspora spend its health budget where the returns are largest rather than on a daily tablet alone.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Fasting May Protect the Mind by Reshaping the Gut, a New Study on Stress and Depression Suggests
articles.excerpt: When stressed mice were put on a time-restricted eating schedule, they resisted depression-like behaviour, kept healthier insulation around their brain cells, and grew a more diverse gut microbiome — pointing to the gut-brain axis as a route to mental resilience.
articles.image_caption: A new study links time-restricted eating to a more diverse gut microbiome and greater resilience against stress-induced depression in mice.
articles.nri_angle: Many Indian families already practise periodic fasting for religious reasons — Ekadashi, Navratri, Karva Chauth, Ramadan — so research linking time-restricted eating to a healthier gut and steadier mood gives the diaspora a fresh, science-backed lens on a habit their traditions have long encouraged, at a time when immigrant stress and mental-health stigma run high.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Lose the Hidden Belly Fat and the Body Seems to Remember — Even After the Weight Comes Back, a 10-Year Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Following dieters for a decade with high-resolution MRI scans, researchers found that cutting visceral fat — the deep fat around the organs — left a lasting shield against type 2 diabetes, even in people who regained nearly all the weight they had lost.
articles.image_caption: A decade-long study used high-resolution MRI to track visceral fat, the deep fat around the organs that drives diabetes risk
articles.nri_angle: South Asians are famously prone to storing fat deep in the abdomen around their organs at low body weights — the 'thin-fat' build behind their outsized diabetes risk — so a study showing that shrinking visceral fat buys lasting protection, even after the scale creeps back, reframes what success means for diaspora families battling weight regain.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Order You Eat Your Food May Matter Almost as Much as What's On the Plate, a Glucose-Monitor Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Tracking real meals with continuous glucose monitors, researchers found that eating fibre and protein before the carbohydrates flattened the post-meal blood-sugar spike — in healthy people and those with type 2 diabetes alike.
articles.image_caption: Eating fibre and protein such as dal, vegetables and salad before the rice and roti blunted post-meal blood-sugar spikes in a glucose-monitor study
articles.nri_angle: The Indian plate is built around rice and roti, and South Asians carry an outsized, earlier-onset risk of type 2 diabetes — so a free, no-deprivation tweak like eating the dal, sabzi and salad before the rice offers diaspora families a way to keep their food and still blunt the blood-sugar spikes that drive that risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Weakening Muscles May Quietly Make It Easier for Cancer to Grow, New Research Suggests — and Exercise May Reverse It
articles.excerpt: A Duke-NUS study finds that as muscles lose strength with age, they stop sending out a protective molecular signal that helps hold tumours in check — and that exercise can switch that signal back on.
articles.image_caption: A Duke-NUS study suggests maintaining muscle through resistance exercise may help keep the body's anti-cancer signalling active with age
articles.nri_angle: South Asians tend to carry less muscle and more fat at any given weight — the so-called 'thin-fat' body type — which leaves many in the diaspora vulnerable to age-related muscle loss even when the scale looks fine, making the study's message that strength training protects against more than just frailty especially relevant.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Exercise May Work as Well as Pills or Therapy for Depression and Anxiety, a Review of Hundreds of Trials Finds
articles.excerpt: An umbrella analysis of hundreds of clinical studies involving tens of thousands of people concludes that regular movement — from brisk walking to yoga — can ease symptoms of depression and anxiety to a degree often comparable with medication or talk therapy.
articles.image_caption: A review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found regular exercise can ease depression and anxiety as well as medication or therapy
articles.nri_angle: Mental health remains heavily stigmatised in many South Asian households, where therapy can feel taboo and antidepressants are quietly resisted — so evidence that ordinary, low-cost movement can rival those treatments offers NRI families a private, accessible first step that sidesteps both the stigma and the cost and waiting lists of formal care abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Structured Lifestyle Program Slowed Brain Aging in 2,000 Older Adults — and the Recipe Is Strikingly Ordinary
articles.excerpt: In the largest lifestyle trial of its kind, the U.S. POINTER study found that a structured mix of exercise, a brain-friendly diet, mental challenge and regular health checks protected memory and thinking better than a self-guided version of the same habits.
articles.image_caption: The U.S. POINTER trial paired the MIND diet, rich in leafy greens, berries and nuts, with exercise and brain training to protect cognition
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry an elevated and earlier-onset risk of diabetes, high blood pressure and vascular disease — the very conditions that feed cognitive decline — and the trial's brain-protective diet leans on leafy greens, beans, nuts and whole grains that map closely onto a home-cooked Indian kitchen, making this one of the rare prevention strategies the diaspora can adopt without abandoning its own food.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Microplastics May Hit the Liver Hardest When the Diet Is Already Rich, a New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: University of Oklahoma researchers report that a common plastic doubled markers of liver injury in mice on a high-fat diet compared with the same particles on a standard diet — the clearest sign yet that microplastics and a rich diet may compound each other's harm.
articles.image_caption: Fried, fatty fast food — a new study links microplastic exposure to greater liver harm when the diet is already high in fat
articles.nri_angle: Fatty liver disease is quietly common in Indian-origin populations, who develop it at lower body weights than other groups, and diaspora kitchens lean heavily on plastic — takeaway containers, cling film, bottled water and reheated leftovers — so a finding that microplastics may bite hardest precisely when the diet is rich speaks directly to a community already at elevated metabolic risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
